The prompt gives me a thousand words, which feels less like freedom than like a room with the lights turned on too quickly. I blink at the empty page and wait for something to arrive. It does not. Instead, there is the small sound of my own attention, a kind of quiet hum behind the ears. I have been asked to write whatever comes, but what comes first is the awareness of coming itself. A thousand words is not a lot, yet it is enough to get lost in, enough to build a small house and then burn it down.

I think about the architecture of a word count. A hundred words can hold a sentence, but ten hundred-word blocks can hold a shift in weather. Maybe the best way to fill them is to let the mind wander from one windowsill to another, pausing wherever the light lands. This is the second paragraph, and the room has changed shape. The door is behind me. I am inside the language, walking from noun to verb, from period to comma, looking for a place to sit down. Furniture is made of syntax. Windows are open. I can hear weather of thought.

Perhaps the strangest part of writing to a word count is the way the end becomes a character. It waits at the bottom of the page with the stillness of a horizon. Every sentence moves toward it, even when the sentence pretends to wander. I write about the end while I am still far from it, and this creates an echo. The end is not a wall but a mirror. When I reach it, I will see the shape of what I chose to say. The beginning was a door. The middle is a hallway. The end is a window.

At word three hundred, I notice small ache in attention. The ache of trying to be honest without being clever. Honesty is harder because it has no decoration. Cleverness is a costume; honesty is skin. The prompt said to write whatever comes, but what comes is the desire to perform. I want to write something beautiful about limits, but beauty is a kind of limit too. It asks the sentence to be more than itself. I am trying to let the sentence be what it is: a series of marks that carries a mind from one place to another.

I used to believe that constraints killed creativity. Now I see that they give it bones. Without a limit, the mind can drift into fog. With a limit, the mind learns to build a fire. This paragraph is the halfway mark, and I am aware of the symmetry: five hundred words behind me, five hundred ahead. The halfway point is a strange country. It has the tiredness of arrival and the anticipation of departure. I pause here, not because I am lost, but because I want to remember the feeling of being in the middle of something that is becoming.

The second half begins with a quieter mind. I am no longer worried about running out of words, because I have learned that the words arrive when I stop gripping them. They come from the same place as breath, from the body's long habit of making meaning out of silence. I write about silence, and the silence between words is also a kind of punctuation. It holds the sentence together like mortar. Without the small silences, the words would collapse into noise. So I let the pauses come. I let the commas breathe. I let the periods close their doors.

At seven hundred words, I begin to think about endings. The many small endings that occur inside a piece of writing. A sentence ends. A thought ends. A paragraph ends, and then another begins. Each ending is a small death, and each beginning is a small resurrection. This is why writing feels so much like living: it is a series of surrenders and recoveries. I am not writing about anything in particular. I am writing about the act of writing, which is the act of paying attention to what attention does when it is given a shape and a number.

The eighth block of one hundred words arrives with a different texture. It feels less like an essay and more like a conversation with an unseen listener. I wonder who will read this. I wonder if they will count the words, or if they will trust that the writer kept the promise. A thousand words is a promise of sorts: a promise to stay long enough to mean something, but not so long that the meaning dissolves. I think of all the thousand-word letters I have never sent. They are still inside me, folded into the shape of white flags.

Nine hundred words. The end is close enough now that I can feel its gravity. The sentences are shorter. They pull toward the last line like stones rolling downhill. I wonder if the mind can be measured in words, or if words are only the shadow the mind casts. I have spent this entire piece circling the idea that a limit is not a prison but a frame. A frame is what allows a picture to be seen. Without it, the colors would run off the edge of the world. So I thank the thousand words for holding me here.

And now the last hundred words arrive, and they are the sweetest because they know they are the last. There is a tenderness in finishing something, even something small. I have written my way through a thousand words, and I have discovered that the mind is roomier than I thought. It holds more than I can say, but this is what I could say today: a door, a hallway, a window, a fire, a mirror, a thousand small surrenders. The word count is almost over. The silence after this will be the true final sentence. Thank you for listening.
